narrative:
The model gave you a 52% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. That is only slightly above an even chance, but it was enough for the law school to treat the risk as too high and deny admission.

The denial was driven mainly by your third-year class rank. You are in the lowest decile, while accepted students average around the sixth decile; this was the strongest factor and pushed the prediction toward bar-exam failure. The next most important factor was your family income bracket. Being in the high-income group, which is rare among accepted students at about 9%, actually pushed toward passing, but it was not strong enough to offset the third-year rank. Your LSAT score of 30 was the third most influential factor and also leaned toward passing, though only modestly.

In practical terms, the model saw your third-year academic standing as the clearest warning sign. For next steps, ask admissions for feedback, speak with a prelaw advisor about whether additional coursework, a post-baccalaureate or master’s program, or a stronger LSAT retake could improve your profile, and consider applying more broadly. Because 52% is close to a coin flip, this is a risk estimate, not a fixed destiny.
